parent.name: King's Gambit
parent.overview: 2.f4 offers a pawn at once to deflect Black's e-pawn, build a big centre with d4, develop quickly and use the half-open f-file against f7 (Bc4, Nf3, castling). The root covers both the Accepted lines (2...exf4: Kieseritzky 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5, Muzio, Bishop's Gambit 3.Bc4) and Declined lines (Falkbeer 2...d5, Classical 2...Bc5, and 2...d6 which is the most played move in the database). Accepted lines are sharp and tactically dense; Black tries to hold the pawn with ...g5 or return it with ...d5/...d6 to ease development. Declined lines are more solid and are chosen by stronger players who want to avoid the chaos. Play is open and double-edged for White's king as well.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Modern Variations
parent.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 d6 3. d4 cxd4 4. Nxd4 Nf6
parent.overview: 2...d6 is a crossroads, not a single set-up. It is the move order that leads to the Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen and Classical/Richter-Rauzer after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nc3 (s4). The open Sicilian is open and extremely complex: White has a lead in development and extra kingside space, Black has a central pawn majority and the open c-file (s1). White often castles queenside against Black's queenside counterplay, giving opposite-side attacks (Yugoslav Attack, English Attack) (s1). 2...d6 also keeps ...d5 off for a move, which is why White has quieter tries here: 3.Bc4, 3.Nc3 and 3.d3 or the Alapin-like 3.d4 cxd4 4.c3 (Tartakower, in the subtree) (s3). The root is described as combative and unbalanced (s2), but how sharp a game is depends heavily on whether White plays 3.d4 or an anti-Sicilian.

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 c6 3. Nf3 Nf6 4. Nc3 e6 5. Bg5 Nbd7 6. e3
parent.overview: Black meets 2.c4 with 2...e6, holding d5 and keeping a secure, compact centre rather than taking the pawn. It is one of Black's most reliable defences to 1.d4 (s1). The price is the light-squared bishop on c8, which is shut in behind the e6-pawn and is Black's main strategic problem (s1). The game then usually becomes a manoeuvring fight: White uses the minority attack (b4-b5) in Carlsbad structures or central expansion with e4 or e4-e5 (Botvinnik plan), while Black aims for the freeing ...c5 or ...e5 break, a Lasker-style exchange of pieces, or a bishop fianchetto (s1, s2, s3). Both Wikipedia and Chessable stress that it is extremely sound yet can turn double-edged when both sides pursue their plans (s2). It was the staple of the Alekhine-Capablanca match (s1) and is played from beginner level to world champions (s2).

parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.

parent.name: Old Indian Defense
parent.overview: The Old Indian (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 d6, here reached by 1.d4 d6 2.c4) is the pre-fianchetto cousin of the King's Indian. Black sets up ...d6, ...e5, ...Nbd7, ...Be7, ...O-O and ...c6, aiming at a Philidor-like central structure that is solid and defensible but a little cramped. The main line is the Ukrainian Variation 3.Nc3 e5 4.Nf3 Nbd7 5.e4 Be7 6.Be2 O-O 7.O-O c6 8.Re1, where theory considers White slightly better. It has never been as popular as the King's Indian; the bishop on e7 is less active than a fianchetto. King's Indian players use it to sidestep the Samisch and Averbakh. The data root also holds the Neo-Old Indian / Modern set-up (1.d4 d6 2.c4 g6), which transposes to King's Indian or Pirc-like structures.

parent.name: King's Indian Attack
parent.overview: White builds the mirror image of the King's Indian Defence: Nf3, g3, Bg2, O-O, d3, Nbd2 and e4, usually against any Black set-up, particularly ...d5 with ...e6 or ...c5. The central pawn push e4-e5 gives a kingside bind and space, after which White expands with h4-h5, g4 and knight manoeuvres (Nf1-e3/g3 or Ne1-g2) towards a kingside attack. Black generally seeks counterplay on the queenside with ...c5, ...b5 or ...a5, or contests e4 directly. It has a modest theory load and keeps the same ideas whatever Black plays, so it is popular at club level, though it is uncommon among top grandmasters today. Black's main dilemma is that passive play lets White have a superior version of the King's Indian Defence, while ...e5 can leave Black behind in development.

parent.name: Four Knights Game
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Nc3 Nf6
parent.overview: Both sides develop both knights, so the root position is a symmetrical, classical tabiya from which White chooses the character of the game. The main branches are 4.Bb5 (the Spanish Four Knights), 4.d4 (the Scotch Four Knights), 4.g3 (the Glek System) and 4.Be2/4.Bc4 quieter alternatives. After 4.Bb5 Black can mirror with 4...Bb4 (the Double Spanish, highly symmetrical and drawish) or go for the Rubinstein 4...Nd4 for imbalance; 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Bb4 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Bd3 d5 leads to an open, more active game in which White usually keeps the initiative. The opening has a drawish reputation and often gives quiet positional play, although sharp variations (Belgrade Gambit, Halloween Gambit) exist. It was almost forgotten after the 1930s and enjoyed a renaissance in the 1990s; Short, Adams and Shirov have played it, and it is popular at club level because it needs little theory.

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: French Variation
parent.overview: 2...e6 is a gateway rather than a set-up: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black chooses the Taimanov (...Nc6), the Kan (...a6) or the Scheveningen (...d6, ...Nf6), with 3.Nc3 giving the Paulsen/Kan/Taimanov move orders. Black opens the diagonal for the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 or ...Nc6/...a6 in a flexible way, with a solid ...e6/...d6 pawn chain and queenside counterplay. The name 'French' is only a naming convention: the pawn structure is Sicilian, not a French one. White's main choice is 3.d4 (about 61% of moves at 2500); rarer third moves are 3.d3, 3.g3, 3.c3 and Westerinen's 3.b3 (Bb2, occasional in the 1970s). At higher levels play is heavily theoretical.
